name: Timurid Empire
summary: Timur’s Turco-Mongol empire, built by ruthless conquest, which later sponsored the Timurid Renaissance of art and science in Samarkand and Herat.

location.value: Central Asia and Iran, with capitals at Samarkand and Herat.

terrain.value: Steppe, deserts and river oases of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, plus the Iranian plateau.
terrain.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

climate.value: Dry continental, so cities depended on irrigation canals.
climate.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

resources.value: Irrigated oases, Silk Road trade and plunder from conquest.
resources.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

disasters.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

urbanisation.value: Samarkand and Herat were rebuilt as great capitals with craftsmen brought from conquered cities.
urbanisation.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

disease.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

migration.value: Timur forcibly moved artisans, scholars and builders to Samarkand.
migration.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

economicBase.value: Farming in oases, trade and plunder from conquest.
economicBase.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

tradeRoutes.value: The Silk Road through Samarkand and Herat.
tradeRoutes.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

inequality.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

governmentType.value: Absolute monarchy under an emir, mixing Turco-Mongol and Persian traditions.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

keyRulers.value: Timur (1370–1405), Shahrukh (1405–1447), Ulugh Beg, Husayn Bayqara.

succession.value: Disputed among Timur’s sons and grandsons, causing repeated civil wars.
succession.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

institutions.value: Persian bureaucrats ran taxes; Turco-Mongol commanders ran the army.
institutions.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

stability.value: Civil war after Timur’s death in 1405; stable under Shahrukh (1405–1447); then divided.
stability.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

eliteConflict.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

armyAndTech.value: Steppe cavalry with siege engineers and war elephants captured in India.
armyAndTech.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

majorWars.value: Sack of Delhi (1398); Battle of Ankara (1402).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Ottomans, the Golden Horde, the Mamluks and Ming China.
alliancesRivals.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

inventions.value: Ulugh Beg’s observatory in Samarkand (1420s) measured the length of the year very accurately.
inventions.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

scienceEducation.value: Ulugh Beg’s madrasa and observatory in Samarkand made Samarkand a centre of astronomy.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

openness.value: Patronised Persian culture, scholars and artists from across the Islamic world.
openness.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

religion.value: Sunni Islam, with Sufi orders such as the Naqshbandi.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

languageWriting.value: Persian for government and literature; Chagatai Turkic (Ali-Shir Nava’i wrote in it).
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

artsArchitecture.value: Gur-e-Amir; Bibi-Khanym Mosque; miniature painting by Behzad.
artsArchitecture.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

socialStructure.value: Turco-Mongol military elite, Persian officials, merchants and farmers.
socialStructure.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Timur’s dynasty and Islam.
sharedIdentity.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

neighbours.value: The Ottomans, Golden Horde, Mamluks, Delhi Sultanate and Ming China.
neighbours.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

ideasReligions.value: Persianate culture spread to India via the Mughals.
ideasReligions.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

colonisation.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

riseSignals.value: Timur took power in Transoxiana in 1370.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

peakPeriod.value: Military peak at Timur’s death (1405); cultural peak under Shahrukh and Ulugh Beg.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Timurid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

declineSignals.value: Divisions among princes and the rise of the Uzbeks.
declineSignals.source: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)

outcome.value: Uzbeks took Herat in 1507; Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

sources.value: Persian chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Timurid Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Good for events; casualty figures from Timur’s wars are uncertain.

knownFor.label: Ulugh Beg Observatory
knownFor.note: A giant sextant measured the year.
